planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Cherokee is a cold-hardy heirloom collard whose leaves take on a deeper purple tinge and sweeter flavor after frost.

directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning or transplanting seedlings to final spacing once they have a few true leaves. Cherokee is a Southeastern heirloom collard carried for generations by seed savers, notable for its blue-green leaves brushed with a purple tinge that deepens with cool weather, along with excellent cold hardiness and a mild, sweet flavor that improves further after frost. Harvest cut-and-come-again by picking the lower, outer leaves while the growing point continues to produce new leaves through fall and winter. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer to sustain steady leaf production, and monitor for cabbage worms and aphids, controlling with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide as needed.

common_name: Old Timey Blue Collard (Traditional Southern Heirloom Collard)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Old Timey Blue is an heirloom passed down within Southern families for generations and is prized for reliable cold hardiness and traditional flavor.

directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and thin or transplant to final spacing as seedlings develop true leaves. Old Timey Blue is a traditional Southern heirloom collard, one of many regional strains passed down and re-saved within families for generations before being preserved by seed-saving organizations, valued for its dependable vigor, good cold tolerance, and classic blue-green collard flavor that sweetens after a frost. Tall, productive plants yield heavily over a long harvest window when picked cut-and-come-again, taking outer leaves while the center keeps producing. Fertilize with a balanced or nitrogen-rich feed through the season for the best leaf growth, and watch for cabbage worms and aphids, managing with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide if needed.
